With her powerhouse voice, dazzling costumes, and infectious energy, she brought Afro-Cuban music to audiences around the world. episodes.title: Are your body clocks off? Meet ‘circadian depression’
episodes.description: What if depression is sometimes linked to your body’s internal sense of time? That’s what researchers from the University of Sydney’s Brain and Mind Centre wanted to know. In a new study, they...
episodes.description_full:
What if depression is sometimes linked to your body’s internal sense of time? That’s what researchers from the University of Sydney’s Brain and Mind Centre wanted to know. In a new study, they surveyed patients with depression whose symptoms may reflect problems with their circadian rhythms – like their sleep schedule, how tired they feel in the morning and whether they’re a night owl. They found that about 1 in 4 qualified for what might be termed a circadian subtype of depression. And while there’s still a lot of research to be done, this could open up new pathways for mental health treatment. NPR health correspondent Will Stone walks us through the study and its implications.NOTE: an earlier version of this podcast had an audio issue at 1:20 — our apologies! if you’re not hearing Gina’s question, try redownloading the episode.

episodes.title: Special Episode: Dr. Colin Elliott & Pox Romana
episodes.description: Having just experienced humanity’s latest pandemic, you might wonder when (not if) the next one is coming. Many public health experts believe we have entered into a new age of pandemics, where...
episodes.description_full: Having just experienced humanity’s latest pandemic, you might wonder when (not if) the next one is coming. Many public health experts believe we have entered into a new age of pandemics, where globalization, land use change, and climate change will increase the risk of pathogen spillover and spread. To shed light on what the future might hold, it could help to turn to the past, to the world’s first pandemic. In Pox Romana: The Plague that Shook the Roman World, Dr. Colin Elliott, Professor of History at Indiana University, presents a scoping and captivating account of the mysterious pandemic that helped to topple the Roman Empire. Using a diversity of evidence, ranging from historical accounts to archaeological remains, climatological research to economic reports, Dr. Elliott paints a richly detailed portrait of an empire on the brink of collapse and exposes the vulnerabilities allowing this pandemic to inflict the extensive damage it did. We remember how the world responded to Covid; how did ancient Romans react to the devastation of this disease? Tune in to find out. episodes.title: The Impossible Trilemma That Hangs Over the Nvidia Crisis
episodes.description: Tian Yang, CIO and manager of the VPX fund at Variant Perception, recently published a report called The Sovereign Impossible Trinity that is especially salient right now. Yang's thesis is that the...
episodes.description_full: Tian Yang, CIO and manager of the VPX fund at Variant Perception, recently published a report called The Sovereign Impossible Trinity that is especially salient right now. Yang's thesis is that the US-China rivalry is exposing three main policy trade-offs: The necessity of sovereignty (which both of the great powers insist on) means that neither state can assure they can maintain the trio of guns (or the AI 'arms race'), butter (social spending), and sound money because of physical constraints, political conditions, and inflation. Given that the US-China AI arms race forms the backdrop of the upheaval at Nvidia, you can't understand Jensen Huang's resignation without considering geopolitical and global economic conditions; his leaving the chipmaker is already a world-historical story. On this episode, Yang talks to us about why Jensen might be our era's Robert Oppenheimer and what it means that the biggest powers in the world can't maintain sound monetary policy while also upholding defense and entitlements. episodes.description_full:
“I’m pragmatic,” Hasan Piker says, when it comes to how Democrats wield power.

Our last episode of the show featured a more centrist perspective on what Democrats should learn from their midterm triumph and what they should do when they take control of Congress next year. Today, we wanted to pair that with a perspective from the left.

Piker might be the most prominent leftist commentator in politics right now. The popular Twitch streamer catapulted to main character status in the recent election cycle, as he took on a more hands-on role stumping for candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and the right tried to turn him into a boogeyman in response.

So I want to talk to Piker about the election and how the Democratic Party should act going forward — especially when it comes to health reform, where I see a synthesis coming into view, and Israel, the issue where Piker is the most personally controversial, and where the Democratic coalition is at the greatest risk of tearing apart.

episodes.description_full: At the end of October, seemingly overnight, a major law firm called Weil Gotshal announced it was winding down after a number of partners departed and talks of a merger with another firm failed. So how did a $2 billion big law firm collapse in the span of a few weeks? In 2015, Yale Law professor John Morley published a paper called "Why Law Firms Collapse," that now looks very prescient, with his idea of a “partner run," or the law firm version of a bank run. What is especially interesting about Morley's paper is his forensic examination of partner-led businesses and the idea that the model might be inherently fragile. In this episode, we talk to Morley about his newly relevant paper, the collapse of Weil Gotshal, whether AI will really change how law firms are run, and the future of big law. episodes.title: The Winning Democrat Who Wants to Break Up Political Parties
episodes.description: Rob Sand will soon be Iowa’s first Democratic governor in more than 15 years. And he won the race in a walk – trouncing his opponent by 11 points, a 24-point swing from how Kamala Harris performed in...
episodes.description_full:
Rob Sand will soon be Iowa’s first Democratic governor in more than 15 years. And he won the race in a walk – trouncing his opponent by 11 points, a 24-point swing from how Kamala Harris performed in the state in 2024. And he ran several points ahead of Iowa’s Democratic senator-elect, Josh Turek.

Sand achieved this political feat by running against the two-party system itself. He campaigned relentlessly on the idea that our electoral system is broken, that the two-party “duopoly” breeds corruption and has corroded our politics. So I wanted to have Sand on the show to dig deeper into his critique of our political system, and ask him how he’ll translate his winning campaign message into actual governance.

episodes.description_full:
Thursday, Nov. 19 will see the release of one of the biggest, most anticipated entertainment properties of the year: The video game Grand Theft Auto VI. 

The first Grand Theft Auto game was released in 1997, and immediately stoked controversy with its aggressively satirical portrait of amoral, criminal American culture. Over the past 30 years, the franchise has continued to keep a sharp satirical eye on American society, and its often unpleasant excesses. The sixth installment promises to touch on hot-button issues like the war on drugs, police violence, conspiracy theories and influencer culture. And yet, even though the game has already made one billion dollars in pre-order sales, it might be the last time we ever see one of this scale. 

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” Michael Barbaro talks with reporter Zachary Small, who covers video games for The Times, about Grand Theft Auto and how it became one of the biggest video game franchises of all time.

episodes.description_full: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, whom US intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, is one of the biggest stories in the world right now. Bloomberg News tech reporter Mackenzie Hawkins has been paying close attention to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based neocloud that Alice Huang was a former executive at — and one of Nvidia’s largest buyers of chips in Southeast Asia. Hawkins is an expert when it comes to the geopolitics of chips, and she tells us that the story that blew up in the last week has been brewing for a while. The US government was investigating suspected chip diversion involving Megaspeed as early as last year. (Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and Nvidia says it found no evidence of chip smuggling.) On this episode, we talk to Hawkins about how she and our Bloomberg News colleagues began investigating Megaspeed and its relationship to Nvidia, the raging debate in Washington over chip export controls, and the incredibly sophisticated and opaque mechanics of chip smuggling itself.
